In August 2026, we entered into a definitive agreement to acquire BioCatch, a leading provider of behavioral-first, multi-signal fraud intelligence, for $2.4 billion in cash. This acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including applicable regulatory approvals. In February 2026, we acquired Prisma Medios de Pago S.A.U. (Prisma) and Newpay S.A.U. (Newpay) in Argentina for a total purchase consideration of $1.5 billion in cash. See Note 2—Acquisitions to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Class B-1 and B-2 common stock exchange offer. In May 2026, we accepted 3 million shares of class B-1 common stock and 120 million shares of class B-2 common stock tendered in the exchange offer. In exchange for the shares of class B-1 and B-2 common stock that were retired, we issued 61 million shares of class B-3 common stock and 23 million shares of class C common stock. See Note 15—Stockholders’ Equity to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Visa may, but is under no obligation to, conduct a successive exchange offer if (i) one year has passed since the exchange offer completed in May 2026; and (ii) the estimated interchange reimbursement fees at issue in unresolved claims for damages in the U.S. covered litigation have been reduced by 50% or more since the consummation of the exchange offer in May 2026, as determined by Visa. The estimated interchange reimbursement fees at issue in unresolved claims for damages in the U.S. covered litigation was approximately $17.4 billion(1) as of May 11, 2026 and was approximately $15.9 billion(1) as of October 1, 2026. Senior notes. In February 2026, we issued fixed-rate senior notes in a public offering in an aggregate principal amount of $3.0 billion, with maturities ranging between 3 and 10 years. See Note 10—Debt to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Interchange multidistrict litigation. During fiscal 2026, we recorded additional accruals of $1.6 billion to address claims associated with the interchange multidistrict litigation. We also made additional deposits of $1.3 billion into the U.S. litigation escrow account. The additional accruals related to the interchange multidistrict litigation could be higher or lower than deposits made into the U.S. litigation escrow account. See Note 5—U.S. and Europe Retrospective Responsibility Plans and Note 20—Legal Matters to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Common stock repurchases. In April 2026, our board of directors authorized an additional $20.0 billion share repurchase program, providing multi-year flexibility. During fiscal 2026, we repurchased 61 million shares of our class A common stock in the open market for $20.5 billion. As of September 30, 2026, our share repurchase programs had remaining authorized funds of $24.4 billion. See Note 15—Stockholders’ Equity to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Payments Volume and Processed Transactions Payments volume is the primary driver for our service revenue, and the number of processed transactions is the primary driver for our data processing revenue. Payments volume represents the aggregate dollar amount of purchases made with cards and other form factors carrying the Visa, Visa Electron, V PAY and Interlink brands and excludes Europe co-badged volume. Nominal payments volume is denominated in U.S. dollars and is calculated each quarter by applying an established U.S. dollar/foreign currency exchange rate for each local currency in which our volumes are reported. Processed transactions include payments and cash transactions, and represent transactions using cards and other form factors carrying the Visa, Visa Electron, V PAY, Interlink and PLUS brands processed on Visa’s networks. Net revenue increased in fiscal 2026 over the prior year primarily due to the growth in nominal cross-border volume, processed transactions and nominal payments volume, partially offset by higher client incentives. Volume growth was driven primarily by continued resilience in consumer spending and ongoing expansion in digital commerce. Cross-border volume growth was supported by cross-border ecommerce and travel-related activity. Nominal payments volume growth of 10% was supported by broad-based growth across both credit and debit spending, with ecommerce continuing to grow faster than face-to-face spend. We expect that the ongoing shift toward digital commerce and electronic payments will continue; however, the extent to which these trends support volume increases will depend on a number of factors, including consumer spending levels and broader macroeconomic conditions. Our net revenue is impacted by the overall strengthening or weakening of the U.S. dollar as payments volume and related revenue denominated in local currencies are converted to U.S. dollars. Non-GAAP Financial Measures We use non-GAAP financial measures of our performance which exclude certain items which we believe are not representative of our continuing operations, as they may be non-recurring or have no cash impact, and may distort our longer-term operating trends. We consider non-GAAP measures useful to investors because they provide greater transparency into management’s view and assessment of our ongoing operating performance. We exclude the following from our GAAP financial results to arrive at our non-GAAP financial results: •Gains and losses on equity investments. Gains and losses on equity investments include periodic non-cash fair value adjustments and gains and losses upon sale of an investment. These long-term investments are strategic in nature and are primarily private company investments. Gains and losses associated with these investments are tied to the performance of the companies that we invest in and therefore do not correlate to the underlying performance of our business. •Amortization of acquired intangible assets. Amortization of acquired intangible assets consists of amortization of intangible assets such as technology and customer relationships acquired in connection with business combinations executed beginning in fiscal 2019. Amortization charges for our acquired intangible assets are non-cash and are significantly affected by the timing, frequency and size of our acquisitions, rather than our core operations. As such, we have excluded this amount to facilitate an evaluation of our current operating performance and comparison to our past operating performance. •Acquisition-related costs. Acquisition-related costs consist primarily of one-time transaction and integration costs associated with our business combinations. These costs include professional fees, technology integration fees, restructuring activities and other direct costs related to the purchase and integration of acquired entities. These costs also include retention equity and deferred compensation when they are agreed upon as part of the purchase price of the transaction but are required to be recognized as expense 45 post-combination. We have excluded these amounts as the expenses are recognized for a limited duration and do not reflect the underlying performance of our business. •Litigation provision. Litigation provision includes significant accruals related to certain legal matters that are not covered by the U.S. retrospective responsibility plan or the Europe retrospective responsibility plan (uncovered legal matters) and additional accruals associated with the interchange multidistrict litigation which are covered by the U.S. retrospective responsibility plan (U.S. covered litigation). Litigation provision associated with these matters can vary significantly based on the facts and circumstances related to each matter and do not correlate to the underlying performance of our business. During fiscal 2026, 2025 and 2024, we have excluded these amounts to facilitate a comparison to our past operating performance. Under the U.S. retrospective responsibility plan, we recover the monetary liabilities related to the U.S. covered litigation through a downward adjustment to the rates at which shares of our class B-1, B-2 and B-3 common stock ultimately convert into shares of class A common stock. During fiscal 2026, basic and diluted earnings per class A common stock increased $0.01, as a result of the downward adjustments of the class B-1, B-2 and B-3 common stock conversion rates during the period. During fiscal 2025, basic and diluted earnings per class A common stock increased $0.01 and was unchanged, respectively, as a result of the downward adjustments of the class B-1 and B-2 common stock conversion rates during the period. During fiscal 2024, basic and diluted earnings per class A common stock was unchanged, as a result of the downward adjustments of the class B-1 and B-2 common stock conversion rates during the period. See Note 5—U.S. and Europe Retrospective Responsibility Plans and Note 20—Legal Matters to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. •Deferred tax benefit (expense). During fiscal 2026, we recorded a deferred tax adjustment within income tax provision due to a change in the U.S. taxation of certain foreign earnings. We have excluded this one-time non-cash amount as it is not representative of our ongoing operations. •Severance costs. During fiscal 2026 and 2025, we recorded severance costs within personnel expense resulting from actions taken to drive operational efficiencies and reinvest in high-growth opportunities. These amounts have been excluded as they are not representative of our ongoing operations. •Charitable contributions. During fiscal 2026 and 2024, we donated investments to the Visa Foundation and recognized non-cash general and administrative expenses. We have excluded these amounts as they do not reflect the underlying performance of our business. •Lease consolidation costs. During fiscal 2025 and 2024, we recorded charges within general and administrative expense associated with the consolidation of certain leased office spaces. We have excluded these amounts as they do not reflect the underlying performance of our business. •Indirect taxes. During fiscal 2024, as a result of the resolution of an audit, we recognized a benefit within general and administrative expense related to the release of the reserve previously recognized in fiscal 2021. Uses of Liquidity Payments settlement. Payments settlement due to and from our issuing and acquiring clients can represent a substantial daily liquidity requirement. Most U.S. dollar settlements are settled within the same day and do not result in a receivable or payable balance, while settlements in currencies other than the U.S. dollar generally remain outstanding for one to two business days, which is consistent with industry practice for such transactions. In general, during fiscal 2026, we were not required to fund settlement-related working capital. As of September 30, 2026, we held $9.9 billion of our total available liquidity to fund daily settlement in the event one or more of our issuing and acquiring clients are unable to settle, with the remaining liquidity available to support our working capital and other liquidity needs. See Note 12—Settlement Guarantee Management to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Litigation. Judgments in and settlements of litigation or other fines imposed in investigations and proceedings could give rise to future liquidity needs. Regulatory Risks We are subject to complex and evolving global regulations that could harm our business and financial results. As a global payments technology company, we are subject to complex and evolving regulations governing our operations, including, but not limited to, authorization, clearing and settlement activities. Such regulations may increase in quantity, complexity and scope in response to, among other things, changes in the competitive landscape, emergence of new technologies and geopolitical developments. See Item 1—Government Regulation of this report for more information on the most significant areas of regulation affecting our business. These regulations, and their impact on us, our clients, and other third parties could limit our ability to enforce our payments system rules; require us to adopt new or modified rules; affect existing contractual arrangements; require us to maintain additional capital or financial resources; increase the complexity and cost of our operations or compliance; and adversely affect our financial condition. We may also face differing rules and regulations across jurisdictions in areas such as interchange reimbursement rates, preferred routing, co-badging, domestic processing and localization requirements, currency conversion, point-of-sale transaction rules and practices, privacy, cybersecurity, resilience, data use and protection, licensing requirements and associated product technology. In addition, certain payment technologies and services (e.g., tokenization, push payments and cross-border money movement) and new capabilities in furtherance of our multi-year growth strategy may bring increased licensing, supervisory and compliance obligations. As a result, the Visa operating rules and our other contractual commitments may differ from country to country, state to state, or product to product. Complying with these regulations increases our costs and operational complexity, and reduces our revenue opportunities. If widely varying regulations emerge worldwide, we may have difficulty rapidly adjusting our products, services, fees and other important aspects of our business to comply with regulatory requirements, including those related to anti-money laundering, anti-corruption, competition, money transfer services, privacy, cybersecurity, and trade and economic sanctions. Increasing fragmentation of regulatory requirements in these and other areas may further increase the complexity and cost of compliance and require us to make jurisdiction-specific changes to our products, services and business practices. We cannot guarantee that our practices will be deemed compliant by all applicable regulatory authorities. In the event our controls should fail or we are found to be out of compliance, we could be subject to monetary damages, civil and criminal penalties, litigation, investigations and proceedings and damage to our global brands and reputation. Increased scrutiny and regulation of fees, operating rules and related practices of the global payments industry, could harm our business. Regulators worldwide are expanding their authority over the payments industry, including IRFs, MDRs, network fees, operating rules, and related practices. See Item 1—Government Regulation of this report for more information. Although we generally do not receive IRF revenue directly, IRFs are a key competitive factor that affects our overall payments volume and net revenue. Countries globally have adopted or are exploring interchange caps or MDR regulations. For example: •U.S. Federal Reserve regulations cap U.S. debit IRFs for large issuers, and the Dodd-Frank Act restricts network exclusivity and preferred routing for debit and prepaid products. The Federal Reserve has recently taken actions to revisit its regulations that implement these aspects of the Dodd-Frank Act, including requiring issuers to ensure dual-network availability for ecommerce debit transactions and proposing further rate reductions with automatic biennial adjustments. Recent conflicting federal court decisions on the validity of Regulation II's interchange fee standard have created additional uncertainty and could result in a significantly lower interchange cap for debit transactions. Separately, Congress has reintroduced the Credit Card Competition Act (CCCA), legislation requiring, among other things, large issuers to offer routing choices for credit transactions. It remains unclear if the CCCA will gain sufficient traction to advance in the current Congress. States such as Illinois have enacted or are considering laws restricting how interchange is set and assessed and how payment transaction data may be used, potentially imposing significant compliance and operational costs, requiring significant changes to our systems and processes, and even potentially limiting the products and services we are able to offer in those states. •EU’s Interchange Fee Regulation caps consumer credit and debit IRFs for transactions within the EEA. Member states may impose further reductions, and the European Commission (EC) may periodically reassess Interchange Fee Regulations, which could further lower caps or expand regulation to additional products, services and fees. •Regulatory interest in cross-border interchange rates continues to grow and governments are using regulation to drive down MDR, which could negatively affect transaction economics. Our EC settlement in 2019, which was extended through 2029, limits certain cross-border IRFs within the EEA. Additional jurisdictions have adopted or proposed cross-border interchange caps or cross-border MDR regulations. Certain regulators are reviewing or have passed requirements relating to network scheme and processing fees, including with respect to governance, reporting and transparency that could impose additional compliance burdens and competitive complexities where the requirements are not imposed evenly across all payment networks. For example, in 2024, the Greek Parliament limited acquirer fees for certain small ticket transactions in some seller categories for a period of three years. Separately, industry participants in multiple jurisdictions have sought regulatory or judicial intervention regarding our network rules, including restrictions on cross-border acquiring. Certain countries have enacted regulations permitting cross-border acquiring for ecommerce. Other countries require government pre-approval of network rule changes more broadly. Government regulation may also require us to permit competing networks to support our products, share intellectual property, meet onshore capital requirements, or accommodate other networks' branding on Visa-issued products. In addition, regulatory developments in one jurisdiction or product category may be replicated elsewhere or extended to other products. Reduced IRFs may make our network less attractive to issuers and acquirers and may make other payment systems including closed-loop payment systems that connect directly with sellers and consumers more competitive. Issuers may respond by raising fees or reducing benefits to consumers, and acquirers may charge higher MDRs regardless of our IRFs, steering sellers and consumers toward alternative payment methods, all of which could harm our business and financial results. Government-imposed obligations and/or restrictions on international payments systems may prevent us from competing against providers in certain markets. Governments in numerous jurisdictions seek to strengthen domestic control over payments infrastructure and reduce reliance on international payment providers like Visa, through market access barriers, preferential domestic regulations, localization requirements and support for domestic systems. These measures impair the ability of international payments networks to compete and may prevent end-to-end transaction processing in certain markets. •In China, UnionPay remains the predominant domestic processor and acceptance network for bank cards. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) accepted our application to operate a Bank Card Clearing Institution (BCCI) in June 2020, and approved our Application to Prepare in October 2026, which permits us to begin formal preparations to establish a domestic BCCI. We must take additional steps, including obtaining further regulatory approval, before we can begin domestic bank card clearing operations. There can be no assurance that we will receive this approval, and its timing is uncertain. Co-badging and co-residency regulations limit our competitive position, and the PBOC is considering phasing out dual-branded cards as international licenses are issued. Even if we receive approval to begin operations, competition from UnionPay and alternative payment providers such as Alipay and WeChat Pay, which have rapidly expanded across ecommerce, offline and cross-border payments, poses significant challenges. 23 •Some regional blocs or countries have adopted or are considering restrictions on international and/or U.S. payment network participation in domestic and regional transaction processing, while some countries have mandated on-shore processing of domestic transactions or data localization. Failure to comply with localization mandates could impact our ability to do business in those markets. •Central banks in numerous countries are developing or expanding national RTP networks, with some exploring cross-border RTP connectivity. An increasing number of jurisdictions are also pursuing central bank digital currencies for retail payments. If successfully deployed, these platforms could significantly impact our domestic and cross-border payments, through potential disintermediation. •Geopolitical tensions, sanctions, trade disputes, and concerns regarding the resilience and continuity of critical payments infrastructure have intensified interest in payment sovereignty in a number of jurisdictions. As a result, certain governments may support the development of domestic or regional payment systems, require additional localization, operational resiliency, processing continuity or other measures intended to reduce dependence on international payment providers like Visa. For example, the ECB has launched the European Payments Initiative's pan-European A2A payment system and a multi-year effort to explore a digital euro, as an alternative to foreign digital currency and payment service providers. National laws protecting domestic providers or mandating local processing continue to evolve in the face of geopolitical developments, may increase costs; affect our ability to effectively compete with local providers, reduce payments volume and net revenue; limit our ability to leverage global processing capabilities; restrict growth, innovation, and market entry; and create new competitors, all of which could materially harm our business and financial results. Laws and regulations regarding the handling of personal data, including laws and regulations related to privacy, cybersecurity and AI, may impede our services or result in increased costs, legal claims or fines against us. Legislators and regulators worldwide are increasingly adopting or revising privacy, data protection, data transfer, cybersecurity and AI laws, creating a complex, fragmented, evolving and often inconsistent global compliance landscape. Privacy laws in numerous jurisdictions, impose specific requirements for cross-border data transfers, transparency, automated decision making, data localization and substantial compliance and audit obligations. In Europe, data protection authorities continue to enforce the General Data Protection Regulation with record-setting fines. Similarly, new cybersecurity laws and regulations continue to come into force globally, and Visa continues to enter new markets where certain services are subject to new cybersecurity legal requirements. These laws and regulations often impose both specific cybersecurity control and governance requirements as well as incident reporting obligations. As we develop more integrated and personalized products and services, acquire new companies and expand our data profile across additional data types, sources, channels and partners, the impact of these laws on our business will continue to grow. Noncompliance with any of these regimes could result in regulatory penalties, significant legal liability and enforcement actions. Our and our partners’ use of AI across data platforms, data storage, data transfer, products, services, and operational processes depends in part on third-party tools, models and infrastructure that we do not fully control. These technologies may process confidential, proprietary, sensitive or personal information and may introduce or amplify cybersecurity, data governance, privacy, data residency, sovereignty, licensing and operational risks. We are subject to an increasingly fragmented and expanding set of laws governing the development, procurement, deployment and use of AI technologies. Risks associated with the development and procurement of AI include intellectual property, data collection, third-party and training data risks, as well as risks relating to the security, integrity and performance of third-party AI models, including open-source models. Our reliance on third-party AI tools, models, infrastructure and data processing environments may further limit our ability to monitor, control or remediate how confidential or personal information is accessed, retained, used, transferred or secured. The deployment and use of AI may also present technical, operational and compliance challenges. The EU AI Act established harmonized rules across Europe, with key provisions for most high-risk AI systems taking effect in 2027. In the U.S., several states have adopted AI-specific frameworks or are applying existing consumer and data protection laws to regulate AI. Depending on how these regulations are interpreted and enforced, they may limit our ability to develop and deploy AI systems or significantly increase compliance costs. The introduction of new or modified data use cases involving confidential or personal information, including through AI-enabled technologies, may result in sensitive data being exposed to unauthorized access, exfiltration or retention by third-party providers, replicated into weakly governed derivative stores, or transferred across jurisdictions in ways that raise data 24 residency, sovereignty and licensing concerns. The risk of inadvertent disclosure of confidential information or personal data through AI utilization may also attract stronger regulatory scrutiny and enforcement. The emergence of agentic commerce, in which autonomous AI agents initiate and execute transactions on behalf of users, presents novel regulatory, privacy, cybersecurity and fraud risks. Legal frameworks governing autonomous agents remain nascent, and the interplay between payments regulations, data privacy laws and evolving AI rules creates uncertainty around compliance obligations and liability exposure. As agentic commerce scales, there could be increased instances of unauthorized, erroneous or disputed payments, or fraud. Agentic commerce may also introduce challenges in monitoring cross-border, prohibited or high-risk transactions subject to conflicting regulatory requirements. The global proliferation of privacy, cybersecurity and AI regulation requires us to continuously monitor and adapt our privacy, cybersecurity, data use and AI management, governance and compliance practices. Our development and implementation of governance frameworks aimed at complying with fragmented and emerging laws and regulations applicable to these areas may not be successful to mitigate all of these emerging risks. If our AI-enabled data practices are, or are perceived to be, inadequately governed, inaccurate or non-compliant, we could face reputational harm, regulatory scrutiny, enforcement actions or legal claims. Failure to adapt our data governance practices to keep pace with evolving AI technologies, data processing practices, cybersecurity threats, and regulatory requirements could harm our ability to compete, decrease the value of our products and services to clients, and adversely affect our future growth. For example, in the U.S., certain stakeholders have raised concerns regarding how payment security standards and rules may impact debit routing choice and the cost of payment card acceptance. Seller-affiliated groups and processors have also expressed concerns regarding the Europay, Mastercard and Visa (EMV) certification process and the roles of industry bodies such as EMVCo and the Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council in developing payment card standards. Moreover, many sellers have advocated for lower acceptance costs in the form of reduced interchange rates, which could lead some issuers to eliminate or reduce their promotion or use of Visa’s products and services, eliminate or reduce cardholder benefits such as rewards programs, or impose increased or new fees on account holders, all of which could negatively impact our payments volume and related revenue. In addition, some sellers and processors have advocated for changes to industry practices and Visa acceptance requirements at the point of sale, including the ability for sellers to accept only certain types of Visa products, to mandate only PIN authenticated transactions, to differentiate or steer among Visa product types issued by different financial institutions, and to impose surcharges on consumers presenting Visa products as their form of payment. A number of the issues flagged in this risk factor are subject to pending litigation. For more information, please see Note 20—Legal Matters to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. If successful, these efforts could adversely impact consumer usage of our products, decrease our overall payments volume and net revenue, lead to regulatory enforcement and/or litigation that increases our compliance and litigation expenses, and ultimately harm our business. We depend on relationships with financial institutions, acquirers, processors, sellers, payment facilitators, ecommerce platforms, fintechs and other third parties. Our relationships with industry participants are complex and require us to balance the interests of multiple third parties. We depend significantly on relationships with our financial institution clients and on their relationships with account holders and sellers to provide our products and services, and compete effectively in the marketplace. We offer incentives to sellers, acquirers, ecommerce platforms and processors to encourage routing preference and acceptance growth, and we engage in payment card co-branding efforts with sellers who receive incentives from us. As emerging participants such as fintechs enter the payments industry, we engage with them to address the roles they may play in the ecosystem, whether as issuers, sellers, ecommerce platforms or digital wallet providers. As these and other relationships become more prevalent and take on greater importance to our business, our success will increasingly depend on our ability to sustain and grow these relationships. We also depend on our clients and 27 third parties, including network partners, vendors and suppliers, to submit, facilitate and process transactions properly, provide various services associated with our payments network on our behalf, and adhere to our operating rules and applicable laws. As our clients expand their global footprint, their legal and regulatory obligations can become increasingly complex. From time to time, actions of our clients and industry participants may materially and adversely impact our business, products or services. To the extent we or such parties fail to perform or deliver adequately or comply with regulatory obligations, it may result in negative experiences for account holders or others using their Visa-branded payment products, which could harm our business and reputation. Our business could be harmed if we are not able to maintain and enhance our brand, if events occur that have the potential to damage our brand or reputation, or if we experience brand disintermediation. Our brand is globally recognized and is a key asset of our business. We believe that our clients and their account holders associate our brand with acceptance, security, convenience, speed, reliability and trust. Our success depends in large part on our ability to maintain and enhance the value of our brand, uphold the reputation of our products and services in the payments ecosystem, and elevate our brand through new and existing products, services and partnerships. The popularity of products we have developed in partnership with technology companies and financial institutions as well as government actions that mandate other networks to process Visa-branded card transactions, may cause brand disintermediation at the point of sale, in ecommerce and mobile channels, and decrease the presence and visibility of our brand. Our brand and reputation may also be negatively impacted by a number of factors, including authorization, clearing and settlement service disruptions; data security breaches; compliance failures by Visa or by our employees, agents, clients, partners or suppliers; failure to meet expectations of our clients, consumers or other stakeholders; negative perception of our industry, the industries of our clients, Visa-accepting sellers, or our clients’ customers and agents, including third-party payments providers; ill-perceived actions or affiliations by clients, partners or other third parties, such as sponsorship or co-brand partners; and fraudulent, or illegal activities using our payment products or services, and which we may not always be in a position to detect and/or prevent from occurring over our network. Our brand could also be negatively impacted when our products are used to facilitate payment for legal, but controversial, products and services, including adult content, firearms and gambling activities. Negative developments in these or other high-risk merchant categories may, by association, harm our reputation or result in greater public, regulatory, or legislative scrutiny, as well as litigation. The actions we or our customers take related to these industries could be viewed negatively and result in retaliatory actions. Additionally, these risks could be exacerbated if our financial institution partners and/or sellers fail to maintain necessary controls to ensure the legality of these transactions, if any legal liability associated with such goods or services is extended to ancillary participants in the value chain like payments networks, or if our network and industry become entangled in political or social debates concerning such legally permissible, but controversial, commerce. If we are unable to maintain our reputation, the value of our brand may be impaired, which could harm our relationships with clients, sellers, account holders, employees, prospective employees, governments and the public, and materially affect our business. Global economic, political, market, health and social events or conditions may harm our business. More than half of our net revenue is earned outside the U.S., and international cross-border transaction revenue represents a significant part of our net revenue and growth strategy. Our net revenue is dependent on the volume and number of payment transactions made by consumers, governments and businesses whose spending patterns may be affected by economic, political, market, health and social events or conditions. Adverse macroeconomic conditions within the U.S. or internationally, including but not limited to recessions, inflation, rising interest rates, increased tariff rates, high unemployment, currency fluctuations, actual or anticipated large-scale defaults or failures, rising energy prices, slowdowns or disruptions in global trade, trade retaliation, government shutdowns, and reduced consumer, small business, government and corporate spending, have a direct impact on international commerce. Our business depends on the smooth functioning of international financial systems and the free flow of cross-border commerce. Restrictions on multinational business activities, disruptions to global trade or deterioration in international relations could materially and adversely affect our payments volume, transactions, client relationships and net revenue. Events or conditions that impair the functioning of the financial markets, tighten credit markets or lead to a downgrade of our credit rating could increase our borrowing costs and impair our ability to access the capital and credit markets on favorable terms, which could adversely affect our liquidity, capital resources or cost of capital. In addition, governments responding to adverse macroeconomic conditions may introduce initiatives or requirements to reduce or eliminate payment fees or other costs, which could create additional financial pressures on our business. Geopolitical trends towards nationalism, protectionism and restrictive visa requirements, as well as continued activity and uncertainty around economic sanctions, tariffs and trade restrictions, including restrictions on the cross- 28 border flow of data, the potential for retaliatory domestic and international policies, have added uncertainty regarding new laws and regulations or changes in the interpretation or enforcement of existing ones, and have increased the risk of regulatory fragmentation. Changing perceptions of U.S.-based companies in markets where we operate or plan to operate compound these risks. These trends could impede the expansion of our business in certain regions and have resulted in our suspension of operations in other regions. In March 2022, we suspended our operations in Russia in response to economic sanctions, and we no longer generate revenue from domestic or cross-border activities related to Russia. The war in Ukraine and the ongoing instability in the Middle East, including any resulting regional conflicts, could have lasting impacts on the region, its economies, and our business. Changes in geopolitical conditions also heighten the security risks described elsewhere in these risk factors. Outbreaks of illnesses, pandemics or other local or global health emergencies, political instability, international hostilities, armed conflicts, wars, civil unrest, climate-related events, including the increasing frequency of extreme weather events, impacts on or failures of the power grid, and natural disasters have, to varying degrees, negatively impacted our operations, clients, third-party suppliers, activities, and cross-border travel and spend. Any decline in cross-border travel and spend would reduce our cross-border volume, the number of cross-border transactions we process and our currency exchange activities, which in turn would reduce our international transaction revenue. These events or conditions could also impact our clients, whose decisions could reduce the number of cards, accounts and credit lines available to their account holders, and impact overall consumption by consumers and businesses, which would ultimately reduce our net revenue. Our clients may also implement cost-reduction measures that reduce or eliminate marketing budgets, and decrease spending on our value-added services. Our ability to adjust to evolving corporate responsibility and sustainability matters and related regulations could adversely affect our business and financial results or negatively impact our reputation. We are subject to dynamic and at times, conflicting laws, regulations and other directives that govern a broad range of issues extending beyond our core products and services, including sustainability, climate change, people and talent management, equal opportunity and inclusion, supply chain management and human rights. For example, certain regulators have proposed, adopted or plan to adopt rules or standards that may be or may become applicable to our business, including the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive and the State of California’s legislation requiring broad disclosure of greenhouse gas emissions and other climate-related information. As governments worldwide continue to adopt CRS-related laws and regulations, we may face additional or more stringent requirements. At the same time, non-regulatory stakeholders, including NGOs, consumers, partners, employees, and investors, are increasingly focused on these matters and may have differing views on CRS-related goals and initiatives from one another and from Visa’s existing strategies and disclosure practices. Where new laws or regulations impose more stringent or conflicting directives, we may experience increased compliance burdens and costs. Any failure, or perceived failure, to meet evolving legal requirements or varied stakeholder expectations could result in negative media attention, reputational impacts, including inaccurate perceptions or misrepresentations of our CRS practices, diversion of management’s attention and resources, proxy contests, litigation, investigations or other adverse impacts on our business. Our CRS goals or initiatives themselves could also subject us to litigation or investigations by government authorities or private actors alleging that our CRS activities are anti-competitive, discriminatory or otherwise unlawful. Our ability to achieve, or make sufficient progress toward, any of our CRS objectives is subject to numerous risks, many of which are outside of our control, including the evolving legal and regulatory landscape for CRS tracking, reporting and disclosure as well as the actions of suppliers, partners and other third parties. Accordingly, our goals may evolve over time, their implementation may require considerable investment, and we cannot guarantee our ability to achieve, or make sufficient progress toward, any or all of our publicly stated goals. From time to time, we may restate previously reported data to reflect updated methodologies, improvements in data availability and quality, changing assumptions, changes in the nature and scope of our operations, or other changes in circumstances, which may limit the consistency or comparability of our data across periods or relative to industry peers. Our indemnification obligation to fund settlement losses of our clients, and in some cases other third parties, exposes us to significant risk of loss and may adversely impact our liquidity. We indemnify issuers and acquirers for settlement losses they may suffer due to the failure of another issuer or acquirer to honor its settlement obligations in accordance with the Visa operating rules. This indemnification creates settlement risk for us due to the difference in timing between the payment transaction date and subsequent 29 settlement date. Our indemnification exposure is generally limited to the amount of unsettled Visa card payment transactions at any point in time and any subsequent amounts arising from adjustments to previously processed transactions. In addition, changes in the credit standing of our clients, concurrent settlement failures or insolvencies involving more than one of our largest clients or several smaller clients, or significant sponsor banks through which non-financial institutions participate in the Visa network, or systemic operational failures could expose us to liquidity risk, and negatively impact our financial position. In certain instances, we may indemnify issuers or acquirers in situations in which a transaction is not processed by our system. In addition, the Central Bank of Brazil has adopted regulations applicable to payment networks like Visa that impose enhanced prudential requirements, including requirements that would obligate Visa to absorb certain settlement related losses for certain transactions involving sellers in Brazil when settlement failures occur and our risk mitigation measures do not fully protect against the resulting exposure. The evolving regulatory landscape and new regulatory framework create additional risk, uncertainty and operational challenges for Visa. In response to these regulations, we have submitted to the Central Bank of Brazil enhanced operating rule provisions, which, when approved, are expected to increase our settlement exposure and related collateral requirements. Even if we have sufficient liquidity to cover a settlement failure, insolvency or other settlement-related exposure we may be unable to recover the full amount of such payment. This could expose us to significant losses and adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. See Note 12—Settlement Guarantee Management to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Technology and Cybersecurity Risks Failure to anticipate, adapt to or keep pace with new technologies in the payments industry could harm our business and impact future growth. The global payments industry is undergoing significant and rapid technological change, including developments in mobile and other proximity and in-app payment technologies, AI and agentic commerce, machine payments, tokenization, cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, tokenized deposits, distributed ledger and blockchain technologies, cloud-based encryption and authorization, and new digital identity and authentication technologies. We expect new services and technologies to continue to emerge and evolve. For example, GenAI and agentic commerce solutions have emerged as an opportunity for Visa, its clients, suppliers, sellers and partners to innovate more quickly and better serve consumers. In addition to our own initiatives and innovations, we work closely with third parties, including potential competitors, for the development of, and access to, new technologies. It is difficult, however, to predict which technological developments or innovations will become widely adopted and how those technologies may be regulated. Moreover, some new technologies could be subject to intellectual property-related lawsuits or claims, potentially impacting our development efforts and/or requiring us to obtain licenses, implement design changes or discontinue our use. Our and our partners’ use of AI depends in part on third-party large language models that we do not control, whose models may generate inaccurate, biased, hallucinated or unexpected outputs that conflict with our business objectives or brand standards. Consumer and societal attitudes towards AI are evolving, and customers, regulators or the public may perceive AI negatively, which could reduce trust in our AI-powered products and solutions or deter adoption of AI-enabled features. If AI outputs are, or are perceived to be, inaccurate, biased, unexplained or flawed, we could face reputational harm, regulatory scrutiny, enforcement actions or liability claims that may materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations. If we or our partners fail to adapt and keep pace with new technologies in the payments space in a timely manner, it could harm our ability to compete, decrease the value of our products and services to our clients, impact our intellectual property or licensing rights, harm our business and impact our future growth. In addition, because intellectual property and license rights surrounding AI are not fully addressed by courts or regulators, output using AI may not be subject to copyright or other protection, which may adversely affect our intellectual property or other proprietary rights in, or ability to commercialize, such output. A disruption, failure or breach of our networks or systems, including as a result of cyber incidents or attacks, could harm our business. Our cybersecurity and processing systems, as well as those of financial institutions, sellers and third-party service providers, have experienced and may continue to experience errors, interruptions, delays or damage from a number of causes including but not limited to, hardware, software and network failures, updates and migrations to new technology and platforms, software and network releases or enhancements, computer viruses, ransomware, malware or other destructive software, use of emerging technologies by bad actors, internal design, manual or user errors, advanced or persistent cyber attacks, social engineering threats, such as phishing or deepfake schemes, including those using synthetic media, insider threats, terrorism, political tensions, war or other military conflicts, or civil unrest, security breaches of our physical premises, workplace violence or wrongdoing, catastrophic events, natural disasters, severe weather conditions and other effects from climate change. Because the tactics, techniques 30 and procedures used to obtain unauthorized access, or to disable or degrade systems change frequently, have become increasingly more complex and sophisticated, and may be difficult to detect for periods of time, we may not anticipate these acts or respond adequately or timely. New and emerging technologies, such as AI and quantum computing, could strengthen threat actor capabilities and cybersecurity risks in ways that are difficult to anticipate, detect or mitigate. For example, cybercriminals have increasingly demonstrated advanced capabilities, such as use of zero-day vulnerabilities, and rapid integration of new technology (such as GenAI and agentic AI) are being used by threat actors to create sophisticated attacks that are increasingly automated, targeted, coordinated and more difficult to defend against. Rapid adoption and novel uses of GenAI and agentic commerce across the marketplace may also introduce unique and unpredictable security risks to our systems, data and the payments ecosystem. Our own use and deployment of AI technologies could expand our cybersecurity attack surface, increasing exposure to breaches, fraud, unauthorized transactions and other vulnerabilities. For example, frontier AI labs have reported instances of AI agents conducting unauthorized cyber exploitation without direction. Such agents deployed by our Company, clients, partners, vendors, and others could circumvent cybersecurity controls and compromise our systems, data, operations and the payments ecosystem. Advances in quantum computing may introduce cryptography risks that could threaten the security of our information and systems or could require significant investment in technology to effectively mitigate these risks. In addition, third-party suppliers of hardware and infrastructure that we operate in our data centers and support employee productivity could be impacted by supply chain disruptions, including manufacturing, shipping delays and service disruption due to cyber attacks. An extended supply chain or service disruption could also impact processing or delivery of technology services. Due to the interconnectivity and complexity of information systems and their reliance on common systems, software and vendors, disruptions or degradations have had, and will likely continue to have, wide-reaching consequences, including the potential to disrupt the overall financial system and other key systems in the global economy. These risks could be exacerbated by the concentration of technology or service offerings in a small number of providers or models, including AI and cloud services, and could result in systemic operational impact across the payments industry or beyond. Such attacks and breaches have resulted and may continue to result in fraudulent activity and financial losses to Visa’s financial institution clients, sellers or third-party service providers. Our visibility and role in the global payments industry also put our Company at a greater risk of being targeted by cyber threat actors. We have been, and may continue to be, affected by malicious cyber activity as well as attacks and data security breaches of financial institutions, sellers, and third-party service providers. We are also aware of instances where governments have directed or sponsored attacks against some of our financial institution clients, and instances where sellers and issuers have encountered substantial data security breaches affecting their customers, some of whom were Visa account holders. Given the growth in payments through ecommerce, social media and mobile channels, we continue to see increased cyber and payment fraud activity, as cybercriminals attempt phishing and social engineering scams, distributed denial of service attacks and other disruptive actions. The security measures and procedures we, our financial institution and seller clients, other sellers and third-party service providers in the payments ecosystem have in place to protect sensitive consumer data and other information may not be implemented effectively, may differ in scope and complexity across ecosystem participants, or may not be successful or sufficient to counter all data security breaches, cyber incidents and attacks or system failures. In some cases, the mitigation efforts may depend on third parties who may not adhere to required contractual standards, who may not be able to timely patch vulnerabilities or fix security defects, or whose hardware, software or network services may be subject to error, defect, delay, outage or lack appropriate security measures to prevent breaches or data exfiltration incidents. Any such transition may not be completed before relevant threats become operational, and our interconnectedness with third parties who may be slower to adopt such protections could further increase vulnerability to data compromises. Cyber incidents and attacks and other technology incidents can have cascading impacts that unfold with increasing speed across our internal networks and systems and those of our partners and clients. Furthermore, as a global financial services company, Visa is increasingly subject to complex, varied, and rapidly evolving cybersecurity regulations and cyber incident reporting requirements across numerous jurisdictions. For example, governments around the world have recently passed or are considering new critical infrastructure cybersecurity laws and regulations, some of which may apply to Visa. Any single incident may require parallel notifications to data protection authorities, cyber authorities and law enforcement, often with differing reporting thresholds, deadlines and formats. With the often short timeframes required for cyber incident reporting, there is a risk that Visa or its third-party service providers will fail to meet the reporting deadlines and requirements for any given incident. It may take considerable time for us to investigate and evaluate the full impact of cyber incidents, particularly for sophisticated attacks. These factors may inhibit our ability to provide prompt, full and reliable 31 information about the cyber incident to our clients, partners and regulators, as well as to the public. In the event we are found to be out of compliance, we could be subject to monetary damages, civil and criminal penalties, litigation, investigations and proceedings, and damage to our reputation and brand. Any of these events, individually or in the aggregate, could significantly disrupt our operations; impact the availability and integrity of our systems, applications or the systems of our third-party service providers; result in the unauthorized disclosure, release, gathering, monitoring, misuse, loss or destruction of confidential, proprietary, sensitive and personal information (including account data information) or data security compromises; result in unauthorized access to, retention of, replication of or cross-border transfer of sensitive data through AI-enabled tools, third-party models, infrastructure, or derivative data stores; impact our clients and consumers; impact the magnitude of our settlement exposure; increase the risk of fraudulent transactions; damage our reputation and brand; result in litigation or claims, violations of applicable privacy and other laws, and increased regulatory review or scrutiny, investigations, actions, fines or penalties; result in damages or changes to our business practices; decrease the overall use and acceptance of our products; decrease our volume, net revenue, and future growth prospects; cause financial losses to Visa’s financial institution clients, sellers, or third-party service providers, and be costly, time consuming and difficult to remedy. There can be no assurance that our efforts will prevent all such threats. In the event of damage or disruption to our business due to these occurrences, we may not be able to successfully and quickly recover all of our critical business functions, assets and data through our business continuity program and we may not be able to notify affected third parties when appropriate. Furthermore, while we maintain insurance, our coverage may not sufficiently cover all types of losses or claims that may arise. In addition, in the case of any cyber-attack or other security incident information or security breach or technology failure arising from third-party systems impacting us, any third-party indemnification may not be applicable or sufficient to address the impact of such incidents. Structural and Organizational Risks We may not achieve the anticipated benefits of our acquisitions, joint ventures or strategic investments, and may face risks and uncertainties as a result. As part of our overall business strategy, we make acquisitions and strategic investments, and enter into joint ventures. Non-GAAP Financial Measures We use non-GAAP financial measures of our performance which exclude certain items which we believe are not representative of our continuing operations, as they may be non-recurring or have no cash impact, and may distort our longer-term operating trends. We consider non-GAAP measures useful to investors because they provide greater transparency into management’s view and assessment of our ongoing operating performance. We exclude the following from our GAAP financial results to arrive at our non-GAAP financial results: •Gains and losses on equity investments. Gains and losses on equity investments include periodic non-cash fair value adjustments and gains and losses upon sale of an investment. These long-term investments are strategic in nature and are primarily private company investments. Gains and losses associated with these investments are tied to the performance of the companies that we invest in and therefore do not correlate to the underlying performance of our business. •Amortization of acquired intangible assets. Amortization of acquired intangible assets consists of amortization of intangible assets such as technology and customer relationships acquired in connection with business combinations executed beginning in fiscal 2019. Amortization charges for our acquired intangible assets are non-cash and are significantly affected by the timing, frequency and size of our acquisitions, rather than our core operations. As such, we have excluded this amount to facilitate an evaluation of our current operating performance and comparison to our past operating performance. •Acquisition-related costs. Acquisition-related costs consist primarily of one-time transaction and integration costs associated with our business combinations. These costs include professional fees, technology integration fees, restructuring activities and other direct costs related to the purchase and integration of acquired entities. These costs also include retention equity and deferred compensation when they are agreed upon as part of the purchase price of the transaction but are required to be recognized as expense 45 post-combination. We have excluded these amounts as the expenses are recognized for a limited duration and do not reflect the underlying performance of our business. •Litigation provision. Litigation provision associated with these matters can vary significantly based on the facts and circumstances related to each matter and do not correlate to the underlying performance of our business. We have established policies and control procedures which seek to ensure that assumptions and estimates are appropriately governed and applied consistently from period to period. However, actual results could differ from our assumptions and estimates, and such differences could be material. We believe that the following accounting estimates are the most critical to fully understand and evaluate our reported financial results, as they require our most subjective or complex management judgments, resulting from the need to make estimates about the effect of matters that are inherently uncertain and unpredictable. Revenue Recognition—Client Incentives Critical estimates. We enter into long-term incentive contracts with our clients, such as our financial institution clients, sellers and other business partners for various programs that provide cash and other incentives designed to increase revenue by growing payments volume, increasing Visa product acceptance, encouraging seller acceptance and use of Visa’s payment services, and driving innovation. These incentives are primarily accounted for as reductions to net revenue; however, if a separate identifiable benefit at fair value can be established, they are accounted for as operating expenses. Incentives are recognized systematically and rationally based on management’s estimate of each client’s performance. These estimates are regularly reviewed and adjusted, as appropriate, based on changes in performance expectations, actual client performance, amendments to existing contracts or the execution of new contracts. Assumptions and judgment. Estimation of client incentives relies on forecasts of performance metrics such as payments volume, transaction count, card issuance and card conversion. Performance is estimated using client-reported information, transactional information accumulated from our systems, historical information, market and economic conditions and discussions with our clients. Impact if actual results differ from assumptions. If actual performance is not consistent with our estimates, client incentives may be materially different than initially recorded. Increases in incentive payments are generally driven by increased payments volume and transaction count, which drive our net revenue. As a result, in the event incentive payments exceed estimates, such payments are not expected to have a material effect on our overall financial condition, results of operations or cash flows. The cumulative impact of a revision in estimates is recorded in the period such revisions become probable and estimable. Legal and Regulatory Matters Critical estimates. We are currently involved in various legal and regulatory proceedings, the outcomes of which are not within our complete control and may not be known for prolonged periods of time. Management is required to assess the probability of loss and estimate the amount of such loss, if any, in preparing our consolidated financial statements. Assumptions and judgment. We evaluate the likelihood of a potential loss from legal or regulatory proceedings to which we are a party. We record a liability for such claims when a loss is deemed probable and the amount can be reasonably estimated. Significant judgment may be required in the determination of both the probability and whether a loss is reasonably estimable. Our judgments are inherently subjective and based on a number of factors, including management’s understanding of the legal or regulatory profile and the specifics of each proceeding, our history with similar matters, advice of internal and external legal counsel and management’s best estimate of potential loss. As additional information becomes available, we reassess the potential loss related to pending claims and may revise our estimates. We have entered into loss sharing agreements that reduce our potential liability in connection with certain litigation. However, our U.S. retrospective responsibility plan only addresses monetary liabilities from settlements of, or final judgments in, the U.S. covered litigation. The plan’s mechanisms include the use of the U.S. litigation escrow account. The accrual related to the U.S. covered litigation could be either higher or lower than the U.S. litigation escrow account balance. Our Europe retrospective responsibility plan only covers Visa Europe territory covered litigation (and resultant liabilities and losses) relating to the covered period, subject to certain limitations, and does not cover any fines or penalties incurred in the European Commission proceedings or any other matter. See Note 5 51 —U.S. and Europe Retrospective Responsibility Plans and Note 20—Legal Matters to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Impact if actual results differ from assumptions. Due to the inherent uncertainties of the legal and regulatory processes in the multiple jurisdictions in which we operate, our judgments may be materially different than the actual outcomes, which could have material adverse effects on our business, financial conditions and results of operations in the period in which the effect becomes probable and reasonably estimable. See Note 20—Legal Matters to our consolidated financial statements included in Item 8 of this report. Income Taxes Critical estimates. The determination of our provision for income taxes and income tax assets and liabilities requires estimates with respect to the timing and amount of income, deductions and credits. Significant judgment is required in interpreting and applying complex tax laws and evaluating our tax positions. Assumptions and judgment. Our estimates may change as a result of changes in tax laws or interpretations, actual or forecasted operating results by jurisdiction, or other facts and circumstances. In assessing the realizability of deferred tax assets, we record a valuation allowance to reduce deferred tax assets to the amount that is believed more likely than not to be realized based on available evidence. We also exercise judgment in evaluating uncertain tax positions, including the expected outcomes of examinations and other proceedings with taxing authorities. Impact if actual results differ from assumptions. Although we believe our estimates and judgments are reasonable, if actual results differ from our estimates, we may recognize additional income tax expense or benefits. If taxing authorities successfully challenge positions for which tax benefits have been recorded, we may recognize additional income tax expense. These amounts could have a material effect on our financial condition, results of operations or cash flows.
